# Opamma Saṁyutta (SN 20)

**ID:** SN 20  
**Section:** Saṁyuttanikāya (sn)  
**Collection:** Sutta  
**Title (Pali):** Opamma Saṁyutta  
**tipitaka.org (CST):** [https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0302m.mul8.xml](https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0302m.mul8.xml)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Opamma Saṁyutta* ("Linked Discourses with Similes", SN 20) is the twentieth collection of the *Saṁyuttanikāya*, situated as the ninth chapter of the *Nidānavagga* [Bodhi 2003]. While most saṁyuttas in the canon are organized by specific doctrinal topics, interlocutors, or classes of beings, this collection is distinguished by its structural reliance on vivid parables and extended similes to convey monastic training and spiritual principles [Bodhi 2003]. It comprises eleven or twelve suttas addressing diverse subjects [Bodhi 2003]. Notable teachings include the roof-peak simile in SN 20.1, illustrating how all unwholesome states converge upon and are rooted in ignorance [Flores 2008; Nyanaponika and Fromm 2000]; the importance of guarded senses and mindfulness, shown by the cat and mouse simile in the *Biḷārasutta* (SN 20.10) [Anālayo 2014]; the power of loving-kindness (*mettā*); the impermanence of life-formations (*āyusaṅkhāra*); and the famous drum-peg simile in the *Āṇisutta* (SN 20.7), which warns against the future neglect of deep discourses connected with emptiness (*suññata-paṭisaṁyutta*) in favor of literary embellishments [Choong 1999; Bodhi 2003].

Beyond the Āgamas, early manuscript witnesses exist: a Central Asian Sanskrit manuscript fragment preserves a parallel to the *Satti Sutta* (SN 20.5 / *Śakti-sūtra*) [Saha 1966], while a Gāndhārī birchbark scroll from the Senior collection (RS 22) contains the conclusion of a parallel to the *Dhanuggahasutta* (SN 20.6) on the rapid fleeting of life [Allon, Senior Manuscripts].

**Parallels and text reuse**

- This file contains 11 suttas; 11 of them have known parallels. Full parallels by collection: SĀ (10), SA3 (1), SA2 (1)
- Examples of full non-Pali parallels: SN 20.2 Nakhasikhasutta ↔ SA3 22 爪甲; SN 20.2 Nakhasikhasutta ↔ SA 1256 爪上; SN 20.3 Kulasutta ↔ SA 1254 人家; SN 20.4 Okkhāsutta ↔ SA 1253 釜; SN 20.5 Sattisutta ↔ SA 1255 七手劍; SN 20.6 Dhanuggahasutta ↔ SA 1257 弓手; SN 20.7 Āṇisutta ↔ SA 1258 鼓; SN 20.8 Kaliṅgarasutta ↔ SA 1252 枕木; SN 20.9 Nāgasutta ↔ SA2 22 食藕根; SN 20.9 Nāgasutta ↔ SA 1083 食藕根; SN 20.10 Biḷārasutta ↔ SA 1260 貓; SN 20.11 Siṅgālasutta ↔ SA 1262 野狐

**Sources**

- [Bodhi 2003] Bhikkhu Bodhi, The Connected Discourses of the Buddha (2003) — Discussed canonical position, classification by similes, thematic content, and Saṁyuktāgama vagga structure.
- [Flores 2008] Ralph Flores, Buddhist Scriptures as Literature (2008) — Detailed the roof-peak simile of SN 20.1 regarding ignorance.
- [Nyanaponika and Fromm 2000] Nyanaponika Thera and Erich Fromm, Vision of Dhamma (2000) — Cited the roof-ridge simile of SN 20.1 on the eradication of unwholesome states.
- [Choong 1999] Choong Mun-keat, The Notion of Emptiness in Early Buddhism (1999) — Discussed the teaching on discourses connected with emptiness in SN 20.7.
- [Anālayo 2014] Bhikkhu Anālayo, Perspectives on Satipaṭṭhāna (2014) — Discussed mindfulness and restraint in connection with the cat simile in SN 20.10.
- [Saha 1966] Kshanika Saha, Buddhism and Buddhist Literature in Central Asia (1966) — Noted the Sanskrit Central Asian manuscript parallel to the Satti Sutta (SN 20.5).
- [Allon, Senior Manuscripts] Mark Allon, Introduction to The Senior Manuscripts — Identified the Gāndhārī parallel to SN 20.6 in scroll RS 22.
